name: Ketamine
short: Open-channel NMDA blocker; anesthetic and rapid-acting antidepressant.
mechanism: A racemic (**R + S**) **NMDA antagonist** at the open-channel **PCP site**, with **σ1** binding; weak NET, μ-opioid and SERT actions are proposed but disputed. Subanesthetic infusions block NMDA on GABA interneurons, releasing a **burst of glutamate** that stimulates **AMPA** receptors and, via **mTOR** or **BDNF/VEGF** release, rapidly builds dendritic spines.

facts.text: Used as a treatment for **resistant depression and suicidal thoughts**.

A model of NMDA-hypofunction psychosis (Table 4-1: **visual** hallucinations, paranoid delusions, no insight). Blocking NMDA receptors on prefrontal GABA interneurons is **acute and reversible**, unlike the neurodevelopmental defect of schizophrenia.

Rapid, sometimes **anti-suicidal**, effects in patients failing many monoamine drugs; benefit usually fades over **a few days** but can be re-triggered by repeated infusions or extended by monoamine drugs. Used **off-label** after multiple failures.
Studied to **disrupt reconsolidation** of reactivated fear memories during psychotherapy (PTSD, anxiety, existential distress in terminal illness).

Dissociative anesthetic (especially in children, and veterinary use); abused as “special K”; far less psychotomimetic than PCP; dissociation (depersonalization, derealization) at antidepressant doses.
Ketamine-assisted psychotherapy explored for craving and use of cocaine, nicotine and alcohol, perhaps by promoting prefrontal plasticity.

updates.title: Esketamine monotherapy
updates.text: Esketamine (the S-enantiomer of ketamine) nasal spray, approved in 2019 as add-on treatment, was approved in January 2025 as **monotherapy** for treatment-resistant depression.

sideEffects.via: NMDA blockade on prefrontal GABA interneurons → glutamate and dopamine excess

name: Esketamine
mechanism: The **S enantiomer** of ketamine: an NMDA antagonist (with σ binding) given **intranasally**, rapidly active without IV infusion.
uses: **Treatment-resistant depression** as an augmenting agent: twice weekly at first, then weekly or every other week

facts.text: A study of up to a year of esketamine plus a switch to an untried oral monoamine drug showed sustained improvement and acceptable safety.
Subanesthetic nasal esketamine for resistant depression; dissociative effects may be harnessed in psychotherapy.

updates.title: Monotherapy approval
updates.text: Approved in 2019 as add-on treatment, esketamine nasal spray was approved in January 2025 as **monotherapy** for treatment-resistant depression.

name: Dextromethorphan
mechanism: A **weak NMDA antagonist** with stronger binding at **SERT** and **σ1** (also α1D and weak μ-opioid). It is rapidly metabolized by **CYP2D6**, so it is combined with a 2D6 inhibitor: **bupropion** (also an NDRI, with possible synergy) or **quinidine**. A **deuterated** form extends its half-life.

facts.text: Listed with PCP, ketamine and dextromethadone at NMDA open-channel sites (Table 3-2).

With **quinidine**: approved for **pseudobulbar affect**. With **bupropion** (AXS-05): FDA breakthrough therapy for MDD and fast track for TRD and Alzheimer agitation (at publication). Bars follow the plus signs in **Figure 7-84**.
A more robust NMDA antagonist than memantine; with **bupropion** (CYP2D6 inhibitor) it blocks NMDA receptors across the agitation network (cortex, thalamus, amygdala, VTA, LC) for **AD agitation**.
With **quinidine**, approved for **pseudobulbar affect** (NMDA and σ actions).

updates.title: Approved for depression
updates.text: **Dextromethorphan–bupropion** (Auvelity) was approved for major depressive disorder in adults in August 2022.

updates.title: Approved for Alzheimer agitation
updates.text: Axsome announced FDA approval of dextromethorphan–bupropion (Auvelity) for agitation associated with dementia due to Alzheimer disease on April 30, 2026.

updates.title: Deuterated dextromethorphan–quinidine trial failed
updates.text: AVP-786 (deuterated dextromethorphan with quinidine) missed its primary agitation endpoint in a phase 3 Alzheimer dementia trial reported in February 2024.

name: Quinidine
short: CYP2D6 inhibitor that boosts dextromethorphan levels.
mechanism: Inhibits **CYP2D6** at doses below those with cardiovascular actions, preventing rapid breakdown of dextromethorphan.
uses: With dextromethorphan: **pseudobulbar affect** (approved); depression and Alzheimer agitation (in trials at publication)

facts.text: Combined with dextromethorphan for **pseudobulbar affect**, by inhibiting CYP2D6.

name: Dextromethadone
short: Open-channel NMDA antagonist studied as a rapid antidepressant.
mechanism: The **dextro** enantiomer of methadone: a relatively more potent **NMDA antagonist** with much weaker μ-opioid agonism than levomethadone. Other binding (5HT2A, δ-opioid, SERT, σ) is less well characterized; μ action might enhance NMDA blockade via **NMDA–μ receptor dimers** (speculative).

facts.text: Listed among the NMDA open-channel antagonists in Table 3-2.

In clinical development (at publication) as a **rapid-onset** treatment for major depression with promising early results. Bars follow **Figure 7-86**; δ-opioid binding (+) has no separate target entry.

updates.title: Development halted
updates.text: Relmada stopped its phase III trials of esmethadone (REL-1017) for adjunctive treatment of major depression in December 2024 after interim results showed little chance of success.

name: Allopregnanolone
short: Acts at benzodiazepine-insensitive neurosteroid sites on GABA-A (tonic inhibition).
mechanism: A **neuroactive steroid** acting as a full agonist at **benzodiazepine-insensitive neurosteroid sites** on GABA-A receptors, which mediate **tonic** inhibition. Details in Chapter 7.

facts.text: The neuroactive steroid listed in Table 3-2 for postpartum depression, rapid antidepressant and anesthetic actions.

A neuroactive steroid acting mainly at **extrasynaptic δ** GABA-A sites (tonic inhibition). Postpartum depression may follow the **fall** in neurosteroids after delivery; a **60-hour IV infusion** may reverse it.
Given IV as **brexanolone** for postpartum depression; neuroactive steroids act at both benzodiazepine-sensitive and **benzodiazepine-insensitive** GABA-A receptors.

updates.title: An oral neurosteroid
updates.text: **Zuranolone**, an oral neuroactive steroid GABA-A PAM, was approved in August 2023 as the first oral treatment for postpartum depression.

name: Brexanolone
short: Cyclodextrin-based IV allopregnanolone; a 60-hour infusion for postpartum depression.
mechanism: A **cyclodextrin-based intravenous** formulation of **allopregnanolone**, a PAM at the neuroactive steroid site of **benzodiazepine-sensitive and -insensitive** GABA-A receptors. Restoring neurosteroid levels after their postpartum fall rapidly reverses depression.
uses: **Postpartum depression**: 60-hour continuous IV infusion, rapid and sustained effect

facts.text: The 60-hour duration seems to give patients time to accommodate to lower neurosteroid levels without relapse.

updates.title: Withdrawn from the market
updates.text: At Sage Therapeutics’ request, the FDA withdrew approval of Zulresso (brexanolone) effective April 14, 2025; the company said it was no longer marketed.

name: Zuranolone (SAGE-217)
short: Synthetic oral allopregnanolone analogue (SAGE-217 in the book).
mechanism: A synthetic, **orally active allopregnanolone analogue**; like brexanolone it enhances GABA at GABA-A receptors via the neuroactive steroid site.
uses: In testing (at publication) as a **rapid-onset** treatment for major depressive disorder

updates.title: Approved for postpartum depression
updates.text: Approved in August 2023 as the first oral treatment for postpartum depression (once daily for 14 days); the major depressive disorder application received a complete response letter.
